llm.reply:
Marfan syndrome is a multisystem connective tissue disease with autosomal dominant inheritance, mainly caused by FBN1 gene mutation, with diverse clinical manifestations [23]. MedGen lists these clinical features: Aortic regurgitation [8], Arachnodactyly [12], Astigmatism [16], Ectopia lentis [20], Esotropia [24], Exotropia [26], Pes planus [27], Glaucoma [28], Congestive heart failure [29] and Hypertropia [30].

## Cardiovascular Features

Aortic regurgitation and congestive heart failure are among the cardiovascular manifestations recorded in the MedGen record for Marfan syndrome [8][29]. These features reflect the connective tissue vulnerability of the aortic root and myocardium that characterises the condition [25: "clinical presentations, diagnostics, complications"].

## Skeletal and Ocular Features

Arachnodactyly and pes planus are skeletal features listed in the MedGen record [12][27]. Ectopia lentis, astigmatism, and glaucoma represent ocular involvement documented in the same record [20][16][28]. Strabismus-related findings include esotropia, exotropia, and hypertropia [24][26][30].

## Diagnosis and Prognosis

The Ghent II Nosology criteria guide clinicians in identifying high-risk patients [25: "The Ghent II Nosology of MFS criteria are crucial in MFS diagnosis"]. Early identification, diagnosis, and treatment can effectively prolong patient life span, as no radical treatment currently exists [23: "early identification, early diagnosis, and early treatment can effectively prolong the life span of patients"].

Marfan syndrome is a multisystem connective tissue disease with autosomal dominant inheritance, mainly caused by FBN1 gene mutation, with diverse clinical manifestations that include cardiovascular, skeletal, and ocular features [23]. MedGen lists these clinical features: Aortic regurgitation [8], Arachnodactyly [12], Astigmatism [16], Ectopia lentis [20], Esotropia [24], Exotropia [26], Pes planus [27], Glaucoma [28], Congestive heart failure [29] and Hypertropia [30].

## Clinical Characterization

Marfan syndrome is documented across MedGen, PubMed, and the literature index under the name Marfan syndrome [1][3], with the entity also recognized as Marfan Syndrome in PubTator3 [4]. A comprehensive review notes that the Ghent II Nosology criteria are crucial in diagnosis, guiding clinicians in identifying high-risk patients [25: "The Ghent II Nosology of MFS criteria are crucial in MFS diagnosis, guiding clinicians in identifying high-risk patients"]. Early identification, diagnosis, and treatment can effectively prolong patient life span, although no radical treatment method currently exists [23: "early identification, early diagnosis, and early treatment can effectively prolong the life span of patients"].

## Literature and Trials

PubMed records addressing Marfan syndrome include publications under PMID 2402263 [6], PMID 35894201 [10], PMID 37058316 [14], PMID 38517496 [18], and PMID 8733052 [22], with titles spanning diagnostic reviews and general overviews [2][7][11][15][19]. Clinical trials registered on ClinicalTrials.gov include Studies of Heritable Disorders of Connective Tissue [5], Comparison of Two Medications Aimed at Slowing Aortic Root Enlargement in Individuals With Marfan Syndrome [9], Angiotensin Converting Enzyme Inhibitors in Marfan Syndrome [13], Losartan Versus Atenolol for the Treatment of Marfan Syndrome [17], and A Randomized, Open-label, LOSARTAN Therapy on the Progression of Aortic Root Dilation in Patients With Marfan Syndrome [21].
